newhorizons.scienceIntro: A brief flyby changed our picture of small, cold worlds. These are three of its enduring discoveries.

science.title: An active icy landscape
science.body: Pluto has mountains, varied terrain and flowing nitrogen ice. The encounter showed that a small world far from the Sun can have a complex geological history.

science.title: An atmosphere seen from behind
science.body: Backlit images revealed haze above Pluto. Ultraviolet and radio measurements complement the pictures by probing the atmosphere's structure and composition.

science.title: A relic of planet formation
science.body: Arrokoth's two joined lobes preserve clues to how small bodies assembled in the early solar system. Its distant, cold environment makes it a valuable record of that process.

instrumentDetails: LORRI is a narrow-angle telescope for fine detail. Ralph combines a colour camera with an infrared spectrometer, connecting the appearance of terrain to the ices present there.
Alice separates ultraviolet light into wavelengths. REX measures changes to an Earth-transmitted radio signal as it passes through an atmosphere, helping infer its structure.
SWAP measures lower-energy solar-wind particles; PEPSSI studies more energetic particles. Together they sample the environment the spacecraft travels through.
Dust impacts generate electrical signals in detector films. Counting these events along the journey helps map how interplanetary dust is distributed.

faq.question: Why did New Horizons fly past Pluto instead of orbiting?
faq.answer: It arrived on a fast flyby trajectory. Capturing into orbit would require a large reduction in velocity and a different spacecraft and propulsion budget. The flyby also allowed the journey to continue into the Kuiper Belt.

faq.question: Why does it use an RTG rather than solar panels?
faq.answer: Sunlight becomes much weaker with increasing distance. An RTG converts heat from radioactive decay into electricity, providing power for a spacecraft operating far from the Sun.

faq.question: Is the trajectory a live radio measurement?
faq.answer: No. Horizons returns calculated spacecraft states based on available trajectory solutions. The page displays their epoch and cache status. DSN activity is a separate snapshot of ground antenna links.

juno.scienceIntro: Juno connects Jupiter's visible weather with the atmosphere, gravity and magnetic field beneath it.

science.title: Storms have depth
science.body: Microwave and gravity observations show that Jupiter's great storms extend below the visible clouds. The Great Red Spot reaches hundreds of kilometres down into the atmosphere.

science.title: A view over the poles
science.body: The polar orbit opened a view of cyclone patterns and auroras that are difficult to study from Earth. Different instruments connect these structures to heat and charged particles.

science.title: Beyond the planet
science.body: The extended mission added close encounters with Ganymede, Europa and Io, bringing new imaging and measurements of Jupiter's diverse moons.

instrumentDetails: Six microwave channels probe different atmospheric depths. Comparing them helps scientists infer how ammonia and water vary beneath the clouds.
JunoCam supplies visible-light context and public imaging opportunities. JIRAM measures infrared radiation, revealing thermal structure and emissions that visible images cannot show.
Magnetometers measure the local magnetic field. Tiny Doppler shifts in Juno's radio link reveal changes in motion caused by Jupiter's gravity, constraining its interior.
JADE and JEDI measure charged particles at different energies. Waves measures plasma and radio waves; UVS maps ultraviolet light from auroras. The measurements are most useful together.

faq.question: Why fly on an elongated polar orbit?
faq.answer: Passes over the poles provide views of auroras and global coverage. The elongated path gives brief close approaches for detailed measurements while limiting time in the harshest radiation environment.

faq.question: How can solar power work at Jupiter?
faq.answer: Juno uses three large solar-array wings and careful power management. The arrays compensate for sunlight that is much weaker than at Earth.

faq.question: Why does the displayed path not always look like a closed ellipse?
faq.answer: The diagram connects the recent states returned by Horizons. Its time window may cover only part of an orbit, and perturbations or manoeuvres can change the path. It is not a fixed, idealised ellipse.

chandra.scienceIntro: X-rays reveal hot matter and energetic processes that visible-light images alone cannot explain.

science.title: Tracing an exploded star
science.body: Cassiopeia A reveals hot debris and fine structure left by a supernova. X-ray imaging and spectra help distinguish material and physical conditions within the remnant.

science.title: A pulsar's powerful engine
science.body: In the Crab Nebula, Chandra resolves rings and jets around a spinning neutron star. The structures trace particles energised by the pulsar.

science.title: Mass separated from hot gas
science.body: In the Bullet Cluster, the X-ray gas and the mass inferred from gravitational lensing have different distributions. Their separation provides strong evidence for dark matter; Chandra does not directly photograph dark matter.

instrumentDetails: Each CCD event records a photon's position and an estimate of its energy. Scientists can build an image and compare spectra from different parts of the same source.
Microchannel plates amplify signals from incoming X-rays. Precise positions and arrival times support detailed imaging and studies of sources that vary rapidly.
When inserted into the light path, the gratings disperse X-rays. Spectral lines reveal elements and provide clues to temperature and motion in the emitting gas.
These gratings disperse lower-energy X-rays into a spectrum. They complement the high-energy gratings and are used with a focal-plane detector.

faq.question: Why must an X-ray telescope operate in space?
faq.answer: Earth's atmosphere absorbs astronomical X-rays before they reach ground-based telescopes. An observatory above the atmosphere can detect them directly.

faq.question: Why are Chandra images so colourful?
faq.answer: Our eyes cannot see X-rays. Scientists assign visible colours to energy bands or combine X-ray data with other observations. The colours communicate measured information, rather than the scene as a human eye would see it.

faq.question: How do mirrors focus X-rays?
faq.answer: X-rays reflect efficiently only at shallow grazing angles. Chandra uses nested pairs of precisely shaped mirrors to redirect them gently toward its detectors.
